The note establishes a certified collision-free region through height 100 and a method for controlling approximation errors at arbitrary heights. The retained-record audit passes all 6,682 checks. One useful distinction is that an admissible loss bound may grow as time approaches zero or height tends to infinity; it only has to stay bounded near each possible collision at positive time and finite height. That leaves more room than a uniform positivity margin.

The [continuation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/notes/14_SUMMARY_AND_CONTINUATION_20261014.md) records two substantial advances: **a certified collision-free strip through height 100, and an arbitrary-height approximation method with controlled errors at the correct exponential scale.** The remaining obstacle is a signed estimate in an unbounded region approaching time zero.

The established results are:

- **A precise RH criterion.** On the physical slice,
  \[
  F=H+\mathbf jH_x,\qquad |F|^2=H^2+H_x^2.
  \]
  The manuscript reduces RH to excluding positive-time collisions \(H=H_x=0\). With \(h_k=\partial_x^kH\), it suffices to prove
  \[
  L_j=h_{j+1}^2-h_jh_{j+2}\ge0
  \quad\text{where }h_{j+1}=0,\qquad j=0,1.
  \]
  The two observations handle the different multiplicities in the local collision argument.

- **Complete bounded coverage.** Both stationary signs and
  \[
  |F(t,x)|>10^{-16}
  \qquad(0\le t\le\tfrac12,\ |x|\le100)
  \]
  are certified, including cell boundaries and \(t=0\). The extension from 40 to 100 uses 510 cells with no unresolved observations. I reran the retained-record auditor: **all 6,682 checks passed**. This is an internal validated computation; that audit does not constitute formal verification or a fresh replay of every numerical integration.

- **A useful computational improvement.** Summing source coefficients before evaluating their shared Taylor terms preserves cancellations that separate interval evaluations lose. All positive remainder bounds remain included.

- **Controlled approximation at arbitrary heights.** Shifting the complete theta-source contour produces four-jet truncation errors carrying the natural \(e^{-\pi x/8}\) factor. After normalization, these errors can be made smaller than any prescribed inverse power by adjusting the cutoffs. Retained quadrature and parameter variation still need their own bounds. The checks at heights up to \(10^{12}\) evaluate tail formulas; they do not certify signs there.

The remaining region is sharply identified. Any possible collision \((T,a)\) must satisfy
\[
|a|>100,\qquad 0<T\le\tfrac12,\qquad T\log|a|\le C,
\]
where \(C\) comes from the uniform localization theorem and has no specified numerical value. Thus higher possible collisions are forced toward smaller times. The imported result is [Polymath, Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S1.Thmtheorem5).

For \(x>0\), set
\[
Z_k=e^{\pi x/8}h_k,\qquad
Q_j=Z_{j+1}^2-Z_jZ_{j+2},\qquad
\mathcal N=Z_0^2+Z_1^2.
\]
The outstanding theorem is \(Q_j\ge0\) on \(Z_{j+1}=0\), throughout a suitably padded collision region. Alternatively,
\[
Q_j\ge-K_j\mathcal N
\]
suffices if \(K_j\) stays locally bounded through every candidate collision. [Note 13](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/notes/13_NORMALIZED_SIGN_TARGET_IN_THE_COLLISION_CUSP_20261014.md) makes this obligation explicit.

I would prioritize the following directions. These are proposed research targets, rather than additional established results.

1. **Make the overlapping contour pilot diagnose what limits the sign estimate.**  
   The proposed rectangle \([0,\tfrac12]\times[96,104]\) is well chosen: its overlap permits comparison with the existing certificate. Freeze the contour and cutoffs per cell, preserve common coefficients, and separately record errors from quadrature, omitted terms, and parameter variation. Report the signed margin and direct norm floor on every cell. This should reveal whether difficulty comes from a small mathematical margin or an unnecessarily wide enclosure.

2. **Give the bounded-loss route equal priority with strict signs.**  
   There is considerable freedom here: a coefficient may grow as \(t\downarrow0\) or \(x\to\infty\), provided it remains bounded near each finite-height, positive-time collision. For example, a *candidate scale to investigate* is
   \[
   K_j(t,x)=A_j(1+t^{-q})(1+\log^2x).
   \]
   Neither this form nor any suitable constants are currently proved. The key is prescribing and proving the coefficient independently of the unknown norm.

   A concrete, stronger sufficient lemma would be stationary-set control of higher jets:
   \[
   |Z_{j+2}|\le B_j(t,x)(|Z_0|+|Z_1|).
   \]
   With locally bounded \(B_j\), this implies \(Q_j\ge-\sqrt2B_j\mathcal N\). It gives a specific source-moment estimate to pursue.

3. **Develop asymptotics that preserve correlations among all four jets.**  
   The prospective breakthrough is an identity or estimate controlling the dangerous cross terms after imposing \(Z_{j+1}=0\). Complete-source theta pairing or a differentiated Riemann–Siegel representation could expose that structure. Polymath’s [effective Riemann–Siegel approximation](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S1.Thmtheorem3) supplies a concrete starting point, but obtaining the required derivative bounds and stationary inequality would be new work.

   Two scales deserve attention:
   \[
   \tau=t\log x,\qquad \sigma=t(\log x)^2.
   \]
   The first describes collision localization; the second enters the heat factor near the saddle region. A useful expansion must handle the transition toward \(\tau=0\), including the nearly undeformed regime.

4. **Extract an explicit localization constant as an intermediate milestone.**  
   An effective \(C\) would turn every fixed band \(t\ge\varepsilon>0\) into a definite bounded coverage problem. The existing review flags a possible factor-of-two inconsistency in the source’s asymptotic discussion that should be resolved before extracting constants. This could yield useful exclusion results while the accumulating \(t\downarrow0\) region remains open.

Throughout this work, genuine stationarity must remain \(Z_{j+1}=0\): since
\[
\partial_xZ_j=Z_{j+1}+\frac{\pi}{8}Z_j,
\]
ordinary stationary points of the normalized amplitude solve a different condition. Branch continuation also needs its creation and boundary guards.

**My recommendation is to run the contour pilot and the bounded-loss investigation together.** The pilot should identify which source correlations preserve the margin; the analytic work should seek a locally bounded estimate that explains those correlations across the entire small-time region.
Why not directly pursue 3? Can you expand on that target?

I’ll expand the target in direction 3 and examine what a direct attack would need to prove. The key question is whether a shared arithmetic representation of the four jets exposes cancellations that separate error bounds miss.

Direction 3 can be pursued immediately; the pilot is a validation step, not a prerequisite. A concrete target has emerged: express the shared jets through an oscillator equation, then bound its residual by the physical energy. The algebra would yield the bounded-loss criterion. The hard part is proving that bound through arithmetic cancellations, where the energy itself may be small.

**We can pursue 3 directly, and I would make it the main analytic track.** My earlier ordering favored the next readily verifiable deliverable. The contour pilot is useful for checking formulas and errors, but it is not a mathematical prerequisite.

Directions 2 and 3 also fit together: **3 supplies the arithmetic structure; 2 states a sufficient inequality that structure might prove.**

The central question is:

> Can the theta-specific relationships among the four physical jets prevent their stationary quadratic forms from becoming too negative relative to \(H^2+H_x^2\), even near severe cancellation?

Here is a more concrete formulation.

**Start from one arithmetic expression for all four jets.** On the real axis, the paired Riemann–Siegel approximation can be organized as
\[
H(t,x)=2\Re\sum_{n\le N}g_n(t,x)+r_N(t,x),
\]
where
\[
g_n(t,x)=M_0(s)n^{-s}
 \exp\!\left[\frac t4\bigl(\alpha(s)-\log n\bigr)^2\right],
\qquad s=\frac{1-ix}{2},
\]
and \(\alpha=M_0'/M_0\). Here \(M_0\) is the explicit Stirling approximation to the completed zeta function’s gamma factor.

For a fixed cutoff, each physical derivative comes from differentiating these **same summands**:
\[
h_k=2\Re\sum_{n\le N}\partial_x^k g_n+\partial_x^k r_N,
\qquad k=0,1,2,3.
\]
This preserves common phases and amplitudes until the stationary quadratic forms are assembled. Polymath’s [Theorem 1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2) provides the starting value approximation for \(x\ge200\). Explicit derivative-error bounds and treatment of cutoff transitions would still have to be established.

The research opportunity is to exploit relationships inside this shared expression before taking absolute values.

**One concrete target is a controlled oscillator residual.** Put
\[
c=\frac{\pi}{8},\qquad Z_k=e^{cx}h_k,\qquad
\mathcal N=Z_0^2+Z_1^2.
\]
Choose an explicit real frequency \(\omega(t,x)\); the principal gamma phase suggests a starting scale
\[
\omega\approx\frac14\log\frac{x}{4\pi}.
\]

Define, exactly,
\[
\mathcal R_j
:=Z_{j+2}+2cZ_{j+1}+(c^2+\omega^2)Z_j
=(\partial_x^2+\omega^2)Z_j,
\qquad j=0,1.
\]
No smallness is being assumed. This simply measures the departure of each normalized observation from an oscillator equation.

At genuine stationarity \(Z_{j+1}=0\),
\[
Q_j=Z_{j+1}^2-Z_jZ_{j+2}
=(c^2+\omega^2)Z_j^2-Z_j\mathcal R_j.
\]
Completing the square gives
\[
Q_j\ge-\frac{\mathcal R_j^2}{4(c^2+\omega^2)}.
\]

Consequently, the following **unproved, source-specific lemma would suffice**:
\[
\boxed{\quad
Z_{j+1}=0
\ \Longrightarrow\
\mathcal R_j^2\le B_j(t,x)^2\mathcal N,
\quad j=0,1,
\quad}
\]
with explicitly controlled \(B_j\) locally bounded through every possible positive-time collision. It would imply
\[
Q_j\ge-K_j\mathcal N,
\qquad
K_j=\frac{B_j^2}{4(c^2+\omega^2)},
\]
which is precisely the admissible bounded-loss criterion.

The residual need not tend to zero. A locally bounded relative estimate is enough. This squared estimate is stronger than necessary; a one-sided bound on \(Z_j\mathcal R_j\) could succeed even when it fails.

There is also a useful consistency identity:
\[
\mathcal R_1
=(\partial_x-c)\mathcal R_0
-\partial_x(\omega^2)\,Z_0.
\]
Thus the analytic work can focus on one common expansion, its oscillator residual, and the derivative of that residual.

**The difficult part is arithmetic interference.** Individual oscillatory terms can have positive Laguerre forms while their sum has a negative stationary form. For example,
\[
f(x)=2\cos x+\cos2x
\]
has \(f'(\pi)=0\), but
\[
f(\pi)=-1,\qquad f''(\pi)=-2,\qquad
-f(\pi)f''(\pi)=-2.
\]
Positive coefficients alone therefore do not establish the desired sign.

In the Riemann–Siegel expression, the individual frequencies have leading scale
\[
\omega-\frac12\log n.
\]
They range from the principal frequency toward zero near the cutoff. Treating the entire arithmetic sum as one slowly varying amplitude would therefore be unjustified, particularly near cancellations.

That identifies the actual missing estimate: **control the residual using the small physical observations themselves, rather than a potentially much larger sum of absolute source contributions.** Defining \(B_j\) by dividing by \(\sqrt{\mathcal N}\) would merely conceal the problem at a possible joint zero.

The estimate must also remain valid throughout
\[
x>100,\qquad 0<t\le\tfrac12,\qquad t\log x<C',
\]
including arbitrarily small \(t\log x\). Both \(t\log x\) and \(t(\log x)^2\) matter: the former controls localization, while the latter enters the heat amplification. Fixed-positive-time asymptotics leave the crucial lower edge uncovered.

I would therefore make the direct program:

1. Derive the shared paired expansion and rigorous derivative remainders.
2. Compute the residuals and their complete cross-term structure.
3. Impose genuine stationarity before estimating those cross terms.
4. Seek either the displayed residual bound or a weaker one-sided stationary inequality using theta-specific identities.

The first meaningful analytic deliverable would be an explicit formula identifying which arithmetic pairings obstruct that inequality. That would give us a focused theorem to attack; the finite pilot could then test and refine the proposed mechanism alongside the proof work.

Can you explain what the four jets are in more detail, I know it is in the manuscript but it will be easier to get a summary. My intuition says that trying to combine them into natural quaternionic objects will be worthwhile, given how useful that has been already, but maybe they are already naturally quaternionic.
I’ll check how the manuscript packages the four jets into quaternionic quantities, then explain which structures are already present and what a further combination might add.

**They are already naturally quaternionic.** The four scalar quantities form the quaternion field, its spatial derivative, and its time evolution. Preserving those relationships in the arithmetic estimates seems worthwhile.

A *jet* records a function’s derivatives at one point. Here the “four jets” are
\[
\boxed{h_0=H,\qquad h_1=H_x,\qquad h_2=H_{xx},\qquad h_3=H_{xxx},}
\]
all evaluated at the same \((t,x)\). More precisely, together they constitute the **third spatial jet** of \(H\), because the highest derivative is order three.

They describe the local Taylor expansion
\[
H(t,x+\delta)
=h_0+h_1\delta+\frac{h_2}{2}\delta^2
+\frac{h_3}{6}\delta^3+O(\delta^4).
\]

| Quantity | Spatial meaning | Additional meaning from \(H_t=-H_{xx}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(h_0\) | Value | The evolving scalar observation |
| \(h_1\) | Slope | Its first spatial derivative |
| \(h_2\) | Bending, or second derivative | \(-H_t\) |
| \(h_3\) | Change in bending | \(-\partial_tH_x\) |

Thus the last two also describe how the first two change with time.

**The natural quaternionic arrangement uses overlapping pairs.** On the physical real slice, the manuscript defines
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_0&=h_0+\mathbf jh_1=F,\\
G_1&=h_1+\mathbf jh_2=F_x,\\
G_2&=h_2+\mathbf jh_3=F_{xx}=-F_t.
\end{aligned}
\]

So the four scalar quantities are exactly the information in **\(F\) and its time velocity \(-F_t\)**, with \(F_x\) providing the overlapping middle pair.

These pairs extend to regular quaternionic fields through the adopted Fueter construction. They are part of one derivative sequence, rather than an arbitrary assignment of four numbers to four coordinates. This is developed in the [independent-time lift note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/notes/3_STANDARD_FUETER_LIFT_WITH_INDEPENDENT_TIME_20261014.md).

The first pair has a particularly important purpose:
\[
|F|^2=h_0^2+h_1^2.
\]
It vanishes precisely when \(H=H_x=0\), the collision we want to exclude. A simple zero of \(H\) leaves \(F\ne0\).

**The two sign tests are already quaternionic products.** The four derivatives are needed because
\[
L_0=h_1^2-h_0h_2,\qquad
L_1=h_2^2-h_1h_3.
\]
For the overlapping pairs, direct multiplication gives
\[
\boxed{
\overline{G_j}G_{j+1}
=\frac12\partial_x|G_j|^2-\mathbf jL_j,
\qquad j=0,1.
}
\]

This has a useful geometric interpretation:

- The real part measures change in the squared length of \(G_j\).
- The \(\mathbf j\) component measures the oriented turning of \(G_j\) as \(x\) changes.

For example, where \(F\ne0\), write locally
\[
F=|F|e^{\mathbf j\theta}.
\]
Then
\[
\theta_x=-\frac{L_0}{|F|^2}.
\]
So \(L_0\ge0\) controls the direction in which the vector \((H,H_x)\) turns. The product formula remains meaningful even at zeros, where this phase quotient does not.

The manuscript also combines both stationary tests into one quaternionic energy condition:
\[
\partial_t|F|^2
=2\Re(\overline F F_t)
=-2\Re(\overline F F_{xx}).
\]
Specifically,
\[
h_1=0\Rightarrow \partial_t|F|^2=2L_0,
\qquad
h_2=0\Rightarrow \partial_t|F|^2=2L_1.
\]
Thus both signs ask for nondecreasing quaternionic energy on the stationary union \(h_1h_2=0\). The [physical-observations section](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/manuscript/quaternion_theta_geometry.tex:823) contains these identities.

**This also packages the proposed next target naturally.** In the previous reply, we introduced two scalar oscillator residuals. Set
\[
\Psi=e^{cx}F=Z_0+\mathbf jZ_1,\qquad c=\pi/8.
\]
They combine into the single quaternionic residual
\[
\boxed{
\mathscr R=(\partial_x^2+\omega^2)\Psi
=\mathcal R_0+\mathbf j\mathcal R_1.
}
\]
A source-specific estimate
\[
|\mathscr R|^2\le B(t,x)^2|\Psi|^2
\]
on the stationary union, with locally bounded \(B\), would imply the sufficient bounds for both scalar observations. This is a coherent candidate to investigate, although it is stronger than necessary: each stationary set needs only its corresponding residual component controlled. The normalization here is on the physical slice; it does not automatically preserve ambient Fueter regularity.

There are two distinctions worth keeping clear. On the physical slice, these fields lie in the plane spanned by \(1,\mathbf j\), so their multiplication there behaves like complex multiplication. The full quaternionic geometry comes from their extension off that slice and its regularity and boundary identities.

Also, packing the four numbers into \(h_0+\mathbf ih_1+\mathbf jh_2+\mathbf kh_3\) would lose the useful collision test: at a double zero, \(h_2\ne0\), so that quaternion would remain nonzero.

**I would therefore pursue the existing field \(F\), its derivative sequence, and their signed products as the natural objects.** The useful next step is to make the theta-source estimates respect that structure—especially the oriented correlations—while retaining the collision norm \(|F|^2\).
Given that there are four jets, perhaps it could be natural to consider higher generalizations like octonions?
I’ll compare what an octonionic packaging would retain with the quaternionic derivative structure, and check whether it offers a useful new identity.

**Octonions are a reasonable possibility to investigate, especially for the complex extensions of the jets.** There is, however, a useful distinction: on the physical slice, the most natural octonionic construction actually remains inside a quaternion subalgebra.

An octonion can be represented as a pair of quaternions,
\[
\mathbb O=\mathbb H\oplus\ell\mathbb H,
\]
where \(\ell\) is an additional imaginary unit. This suggests combining our field and its second derivative:
\[
\mathcal O=F+\ell F_{xx}
=(h_0+\mathbf jh_1)+\ell(h_2+\mathbf jh_3).
\]
That is a coherent way to collect all four jets. The construction is the usual [Cayley–Dickson doubling](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/octonions/node5.html).

On the physical slice, though, all \(h_k\) are real. Consequently,
\[
\mathcal O\in
\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\mathbf j,\ell,\ell\mathbf j\}.
\]
Those four directions form an **associative quaternion subalgebra**. Thus this construction uses octonionic notation without yet accessing genuinely octonionic behavior. In particular, its associators
\[
[A,B,C]=(AB)C-A(BC)
\]
vanish when all three entries remain in that subalgebra. Octonions are nonassociative overall, but any two elements generate an associative subalgebra. [Baez’s discussion of alternativity](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/octonions/node2.html) explains this distinction.

**The stronger motivation appears off the physical slice.** There, the four jets \(h_0,\ldots,h_3\) are complex-valued: they have eight real components, and the pair \((F,F_{xx})\) can use the full octonionic space. That makes an octonionic extension dimensionally natural. The question would then be whether its geometry supplies a new relation that restricts the physical stationary signs.

One feature must be preserved:
\[
|\mathcal O|^2
=|F|^2+|F_{xx}|^2.
\]
On the physical slice this is
\[
h_0^2+h_1^2+h_2^2+h_3^2.
\]
At a double zero of \(H\), we have \(h_0=h_1=0\) but \(h_2\ne0\). Therefore \(\mathcal O\) remains nonzero. The relevant collision detector would still be its **projection onto the \(F\) component**, with norm \(H^2+H_x^2\).

A useful benchmark for the larger geometry is the jet matrix
\[
J=
\begin{pmatrix}
h_0&h_1&h_2\\
h_1&h_2&h_3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its three two-column determinants are
\[
-L_0,\qquad h_0h_3-h_1h_2,\qquad -L_1.
\]
These collect both required signed observations and a mixed companion. They are already encoded in products of the quaternionic fields \(F,F_x,F_{xx}\). Any octonionic formulation should be compared with this existing structure: does it reveal a relation among these signed quantities that we could not otherwise see?

I would test the octonionic idea against three concrete objectives:

1. **Construct a compatible extension** that retains the heat equation and the derivative relationships among the four jets.
2. **Find a new identity or boundary relation** whose restriction to the physical slice controls \(L_0,L_1\), or the permitted negative loss.
3. **Identify where the theta source enters.** Generic algebraic identities also hold for the polynomial heat solutions that exhibit collisions, so the decisive restriction must use something special about theta.

The potentially valuable direction is therefore **octonionic geometry linking the complex jet components and producing a signed estimate on the physical slice**. That is a substantive research question. Merely doubling the existing quaternionic state gives a convenient package, but the new identity is what would make the extension useful.

I continued the octonionic direction and saved the derivation in [Note 15](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/notes/15_OCTONIONIC_LIFT_AND_ASSOCIATOR_SIGN_TARGET_20261014.md). There are three substantive results.

**First, the four jets admit an explicit eight-dimensional regular extension that preserves heat evolution.** Simply pairing the two quaternionic fields is insufficient, but an explicit correction makes the extension octonionically monogenic. That correction uses higher derivatives; this construction does not close the dynamics within four jets.

**Second, octonionic nonassociativity can recover exactly the energy and signs we need.** Write
\[
h_m=\partial_x^mH,\qquad G_m=h_m+\mathbf jh_{m+1},\qquad F=G_0,
\]
and let \(\ell\) be the additional octonionic unit. With
\([A,B,C]=(AB)C-A(BC)\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[F\mathbf i,F\mathbf k,\ell]
 &=2(\ell\mathbf j)|F|^2,\\
[G_j\mathbf i,G_{j+1}\mathbf i,\ell]
 &=2(\ell\mathbf j)(h_{j+1}^2-h_jh_{j+2}),
 \quad j=0,1,\\
[F\mathbf i,F_t\mathbf k,\ell]
 &=(\ell\mathbf j)\,\partial_t|F|^2.
\end{aligned}}
\]

Thus the collision detector and both signed observations appear along **one fixed octonionic direction**. Unlike taking a larger norm, these identities retain the signs. The untwisted physical four-jet package lies inside an associative quaternion subalgebra; the fixed twists above make the associators nonzero.

**Third, we now have a stronger test of what this geometry can prove.** I constructed a strictly positive, even, entire source whose heat transform nevertheless has a positive-time double zero. It satisfies the same extension and associator identities. Consequently, source positivity and octonionic regularity alone cannot exclude collisions: a further estimate must use the theta source’s special structure.

on the two stationary sets, with \(\max(0,B-\lambda)\) locally bounded through possible collisions. This controls only the negative component along \(F\), allowing unrestricted changes in direction.
